analysis.one_liner: Carbon tax funding infrastructure, replacing fuel taxes, with EPA rules paused.
analysis.headline: Bipartisan carbon-tax bill never got a committee vote; no floor action was ever scheduled
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 3039 would put a price of $35 per ton on greenhouse gas emissions, replacing federal gas and jet-fuel taxes. Revenue funds roads, aid to low-income households facing higher energy costs, and displaced fossil-fuel workers. In exchange, EPA regulation of greenhouse gases is paused through 2034 unless emissions targets are missed.
analysis.who_benefits: Infrastructure users and highway funding, low-income households receiving energy-cost rebates, fossil-fuel workers getting transition aid, and industries preferring a predictable carbon price over regulatory uncertainty

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a $35-per-ton tax on greenhouse gas emissions, rising over time, replacing existing gas and jet-fuel taxes [S2]
Sends 70% of revenue to the Highway Trust Fund, addressing the chronic shortfall in road and bridge maintenance [S3]
Provides grants to low-income households to offset energy costs [S2]
Funds worker retraining, early retirement, health benefits, and community economic redevelopment for fossil-fuel and nuclear workers displaced by the policy [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Fossil-fuel producers, heavy industry, and ultimately consumers of energy and carbon-intensive goods, who face higher prices; also EPA regulatory authority, which is suspended until emissions targets are missed or 2035

drawbacks.text: Puts federal greenhouse gas regulation on hold until 2035, leaving emissions control dependent solely on the tax's price signal [S2]
Energy costs rise for consumers; the bill offsets them only for households under 150% of the poverty line, leaving moderate-income families unprotected [S3]
The tax rate escalator (5 percentage points plus inflation) applies automatically and is locked into statute, limiting future flexibility if economic conditions change [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A genuine bipartisan attempt to pair carbon pricing with tangible household and worker protections and infrastructure investment. But the regulatory moratorium is a major concession, and the consumer protection covers only the very lowest-income households. Overall a serious, mixed-effort proposal rather than a giveaway.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to seven House committees and never moved; no markup, no floor vote, and the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Introduced May 7, 2021 by Rep. Fitzpatrick with Rep. Carbajal as a bipartisan cosponsor [S1]
Referred to seven committees, including Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure [S1]
No further action was taken after subcommittee referrals; no markup or vote ever occurred [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's death in a direct material sense, but the status quo benefited: fossil-fuel interests and auto/oil-linked industries avoided a new carbon price, and EPA kept its existing regulatory authority intact. Infrastructure funding remained on its existing path rather than the RISE Trust Fund model.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.role: House sponsor, Problem Solvers Caucus member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought bipartisan cosponsorship from across the aisle

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the sole cosponsor, giving the bill its bipartisan pair

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, never scheduled a markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on day one and never took it up; without a markup it could not reach the floor

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority party, controlled the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor time; the bill sat through the entire 117th Congress

against.name: Fossil-fuel and transportation industries
against.role: Industries facing a new carbon tax
against.what_they_did: The bill faced the standard industry resistance to carbon pricing; no public evidence of a specific campaign in this record

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, a classic cross-party pairing; the bill never advanced far enough to test broader party support.

industries.note: They would pay a new $35-per-ton emissions tax but gain a moratorium on EPA greenhouse gas rules and a predictable price instead of regulatory uncertainty. For ordinary people this is a trade of a strong regulatory backstop for a market price plus limited household relief.
70% of revenue flows to the Highway Trust Fund, expanding road and bridge work. Ordinary drivers also benefit from better roads, though their costs rise at the pump.
Repeal of federal gas and jet-fuel taxes is offset for consumers by the carbon tax on fuels, so the net effect on drivers is not clearly favorable.
